introduction-the-run-button-for-infrastr.core: A Makefile gives every project the same short entry points (`make test`, `make deploy`) wrapping the long, fragile commands only one person remembers. It's the project's run button.

first_principles.problem: Deploying requires a 120-character terraform command with the right var-file that lives only in someone's shell history.
truths: Long commands get forgotten or mistyped.
Consistent entry points help humans and CI alike.
derivation: Use the **same targets locally and in CI**.
Keep the logic in scripts; Make **orchestrates**.

analogy.title: A TV remote's labelled buttons
analogy.story: You press 'Netflix' instead of typing the input sequence every time.
analogy.breaks: Make isn't a full programming language, so complex logic belongs in scripts.

example.title: A new teammate's first deploy
example.outcome: a universal interface for every project.

check.q: What's the main benefit of a Makefile in DevOps repos?
check.a: Consistent, discoverable entry points for complex commands, shared by humans and CI.

anatomy-of-a-makefile.core: A Makefile is a set of rules: `target: prerequisites` followed by TAB-indented recipe lines. Variables (`VAR ?= default`) and automatic variables reduce repetition.

first_principles.problem: Make's syntax trips people up: spaces instead of tabs fail with a cryptic 'missing separator'.
truths: Make was built for file dependencies.
Recipes must start with a tab character.
Each recipe line runs in a separate shell.
derivation: Use **VAR ?= default** and **$(VAR)** to use it.
Each line is a **new shell**: chain with && or use .ONESHELL.
Prefix with **@** to hide the command echo.

analogy.title: A recipe card
analogy.story: Dish name (target), what you must prepare first (prerequisites), and the numbered steps (recipe).
analogy.breaks: `cd dir` on one line doesn't affect the next line, because each line is a separate shell.

example.title: A small Makefile

steps.label: Run
steps.detail: `make test` builds first because of the prerequisite.

code.text:
IMAGE ?= myapp
TAG   ?= dev

build:
	docker build -t $(IMAGE):$(TAG) .

test: build
	docker run --rm $(IMAGE):$(TAG) pytest

example.outcome: you can read and write Makefiles confidently.

check.q: Why does `cd build` on one recipe line not affect the next line?
check.a: Each recipe line runs in its own shell process.

the-phony-declaration.core: Make assumes targets are files. If a file named `test` exists and is up to date, `make test` does nothing. Declaring `.PHONY: test` tells Make the target is an action that always runs.

first_principles.problem: Someone creates a `test/` directory and `make test` silently stops running the tests.
truths: Make skips targets whose file is newer than its deps.
DevOps targets are actions, not files.
derivation: Keep **file targets** for real artifacts (for caching).
Declare them near the top or next to each target.

analogy.title: A 'do it anyway' sticker
analogy.story: Normally the robot skips a job if the output already exists. The sticker says this job is an action, not a product, so always do it.
analogy.breaks: Making everything phony loses Make's incremental-build benefits for real files.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: `make test` always runs, whether or not a test/ directory exists.

check.q: What happens to `make clean` if a file named clean exists and clean isn't phony?
check.a: Make reports it as up to date and doesn't run the recipe.

environment-injection-and-cicd-integrati.core: Make variables come from the Makefile, environment variables or the command line, in increasing precedence. With `?=` defaults the same Makefile serves laptops and CI pipelines.

first_principles.problem: Hard-coded values make the Makefile unusable across environments and in pipelines.
truths: CI injects values through the environment.
Humans pass overrides on the command line.

analogy.title: A form with defaults, preferences and explicit choices
analogy.story: Defaults are pre-filled, your saved preferences replace them, and what you type now wins.
analogy.breaks: `=` vs `:=` vs `?=` behave differently. `?=` only sets the value if it isn't already set.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Identical logic everywhere, with only the inputs changing.

code.text:
ENV ?= dev
TAG ?= $(shell git rev-parse --short HEAD)

deploy:
	@test -n "$(ENV)" || (echo "ENV required"; exit 1)
	helm upgrade app ./chart -f values-$(ENV).yaml --set image.tag=$(TAG)

# CI: make deploy ENV=prod TAG=$GITHUB_SHA

check.q: Which wins: an env var or `make VAR=x`?

makefile-patterns-for-real-projects.core: Proven patterns include a self-documenting `help` target that parses `## comments`, `.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`, guard targets for required variables, `include` for shared fragments and `$(MAKE) -C` for subprojects.

first_principles.problem: Team Makefiles grow into undocumented, copy-pasted tangles.
truths: Docs next to code stay current.
Shared logic should be included once.
derivation: Annotate targets with **## description** and generate **help** from them.

analogy.title: A building directory in the lobby
analogy.story: The directory lists every office automatically from the door plaques, so it's never out of date.
analogy.breaks: Clever Make tricks can get unreadable, so prefer clarity.

example.title: The self-documenting help target

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Running bare `make` lists every target with its description.

code.text:
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help
.PHONY: help
help: ## Show this help
	@grep -E '^[a-zA-Z_-]+:.*?## ' $(MAKEFILE_LIST) | awk 'BEGIN{FS=":.*?## "}{printf "  %-12s %s\n", $$1, $$2}'

plan: ## Terraform plan for ENV
	terraform plan -var-file=$(ENV).tfvars

example.outcome: Makefiles that document and protect themselves.

check.a: So running bare `make` shows the help instead of accidentally running the first real target.
